name: Peter
title: One of the Twelve
tagline: A fisherman from Bethsaida, named first in every list of the Twelve.
story: A fisherman from Bethsaida whom Jesus named Cephas, or Peter; named first in every list of the Twelve, he denied Jesus three times and spoke for the apostles.

periods.title: With Jesus
periods.sub: The Gospels, in the harmony’s order

entries.title: From Bethsaida; a house at Capernaum
entries.text: Scripture says Philip “was of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter” (John 1:44). In Capernaum Simon and Andrew had a house (Mark 1:21, 29), which Matthew calls “Peter’s house” (Matt 8:14).

entries.title: A fisherman with Andrew
entries.text: A fisherman, casting a net with his brother Andrew (Matt 4:18). James and John, the sons of Zebedee, were his “partners” (Luke 5:10).

entries.title: Andrew’s brother
entries.text: His brother was Andrew, who brought him to Jesus (John 1:40–42).

entries.title: The son of Jona
entries.text: His father is called Jona (John 1:42) and Jonas (John 21:15–17); Jesus calls him “Simon Bar-jona”, son of Jona (Matt 16:17).

entries.title: A married man
entries.text: He was married. Jesus healed “Simon’s wife’s mother” at his house (Mark 1:29–31), and Paul says Cephas took “a wife” with him on his travels (1 Cor 9:5). Scripture does not give her name or mention children.

entries.title: Children, says Clement
entries.text: Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200), as quoted by Eusebius, says that Peter had children, and that “they say” Peter saw his own wife led out to die and called to her, “Remember the Lord.”

entries.title: Brought to Jesus by Andrew and named Cephas

entries.title: Choosing a twelfth apostle
entries.text: He stands up among about 120 believers and leads the choosing of one to take Judas’s place (Acts 1:15–26).

entries.title: Pentecost
entries.text: At Pentecost he speaks for the Eleven (“Peter, standing up with the eleven”), and about three thousand are baptized (Acts 2:14–41).

entries.title: The lame man at the temple gate
entries.text: With John he heals a lame man at the temple gate and speaks in Solomon’s porch (Acts 3:1–26).

entries.title: Arrested with John
entries.text: He and John are arrested and questioned by the council, who see that they are “unlearned and ignorant men” and that “they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:1–22).

entries.title: Ananias and Sapphira; the council
entries.text: He confronts Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–11). People lay the sick in the streets so that “the shadow of Peter passing by” might fall on them (Acts 5:15). Before the council, “Peter and the other apostles” say, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

entries.title: Sent to Samaria
entries.text: He is sent with John to Samaria, where they lay hands on the new believers and Peter rebukes Simon the sorcerer (Acts 8:14–25).

entries.title: Lydda and Joppa
entries.text: At Lydda he heals Aeneas; at Joppa he raises Tabitha and stays with Simon a tanner (Acts 9:32–43).

entries.title: Cornelius at Caesarea
entries.text: After a vision at Joppa he goes to the Roman centurion Cornelius at Caesarea, and the Holy Ghost falls on Gentiles (Acts 10:1–48). He defends this in Jerusalem (Acts 11:1–18).

entries.title: Prison, and the angel
entries.text: Herod kills James and then imprisons Peter; an angel leads him out. He goes to the house of Mary the mother of John Mark, then “departed, and went into another place” (Acts 12:3–17).

entries.title: The council at Jerusalem
entries.text: At the council in Jerusalem he speaks for receiving the Gentiles (Acts 15:7–11). This is the last time Acts names him.

entries.title: Paul stays fifteen days; the pillars
entries.text: Paul went up to Jerusalem “to see Peter, and abode with him fifteen days” (Gal 1:18). Later James, Cephas and John “seemed to be pillars” and gave Paul and Barnabas “the right hands of fellowship” (Gal 2:9).

entries.title: Withstood at Antioch
entries.text: At Antioch Paul “withstood him to the face” for withdrawing from eating with Gentiles (Gal 2:11–14).

entries.title: A wife on his travels; “I of Cephas”
entries.text: Paul says Cephas travelled with a wife (1 Cor 9:5), and some at Corinth said “I of Cephas” (1 Cor 1:12).

entries.title: “By Silvanus … at Babylon”
entries.text: 1 Peter is written “By Silvanus” and sends greetings from the church “at Babylon” and from “Marcus my son” (1 Pet 5:12–13).

entries.title: Clement of Rome, 1 Clement 5
entries.text: Peter “endured not one nor two but many labours, and thus having borne his testimony went to his appointed place of glory.” No place and no manner of death is given.
entries.when: about AD 95–96, at the close of Domitian’s persecution (Lightfoot, 1891)

entries.title: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Romans 4
entries.text: Writing to the Roman church on his way to death, Ignatius says, “I do not enjoin you, as Peter and Paul did.”
entries.who: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Romans 4

entries.title: Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, letter to the Romans, quoted by Eusebius (2.25.8)
entries.text: Peter and Paul “taught together in like manner in Italy, and suffered martyrdom at the same time.”
entries.who: Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, letter to the Romans, quoted by Eusebius (2.25.8)
entries.when: about AD 170, writing to Soter, bishop of Rome (Eusebius 4.23.9)

entries.title: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1
entries.text: Matthew wrote “while Peter and Paul were preaching at Rome, and laying the foundations of the Church”, and Mark was “the disciple and interpreter of Peter”.

entries.title: The Muratorian fragment, an anonymous list of New Testament books
entries.text: Luke’s Acts leaves out “the passion of Peter” because Luke wrote only what he saw himself.
entries.who: The Muratorian fragment, an anonymous list of New Testament books

entries.title: Gaius (Caius) of Rome, against Proclus, quoted by Eusebius (2.25.7)
entries.text: “I can show the trophies of the apostles. For if you will go to the Vatican or to the Ostian way, you will find the trophies of those who laid the foundations of this church.”
entries.who: Gaius (Caius) of Rome, against Proclus, quoted by Eusebius (2.25.7)
entries.when: about AD 200 (under Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome)

entries.title: Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics 36 and Scorpiace 15
entries.text: At Rome, “Peter endures a passion like his Lord’s”; elsewhere, “Then is Peter girt by another, when he is made fast to the cross.”
entries.who: Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics 36 and Scorpiace 15

entries.title: The Acts of Peter (apocryphal), chs. 35–37
entries.text: Leaving Rome, Peter meets the Lord and asks, “Lord, whither goest thou”; told “I go into Rome to be crucified”, he turns back. He asks to be crucified “with the head downward and not otherwise”.
entries.when: not later than AD 200 (M. R. James, 1924)

claim.text: His brother, who brought him to Jesus (John 1:40–42). They fished together and shared a house (Mark 1:16, 29).
A fishing partner (Luke 5:10). With Peter and John, one of the three Jesus took into Jairus’s house, up the mountain, and further into Gethsemane (Mark 5:37; 9:2; 14:33).
A fishing partner (Luke 5:10), sent with Peter to prepare the passover (Luke 22:8), and with him at the temple, before the council and in Samaria (Acts 3:1; 4:13; 8:14).
Paul says Cephas took “a wife” with him (1 Cor 9:5).
The centurion at Caesarea who sent for Peter (Acts 10:1–8, 24–48).
Paul stayed with him fifteen days in Jerusalem, and later opposed him at Antioch (Gal 1:18; 2:11).
On his visit to Peter, Paul saw no other apostle “save James the Lord’s brother” (Gal 1:19).

Freed from prison, Peter went to the house of Mary, “the mother of John, whose surname was Mark” (Acts 12:12). 1 Peter sends greetings from “Marcus my son” (1 Pet 5:13); our people data treats the two as one man.
Papias (early 2nd century), quoted by Eusebius, says Mark “having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately … whatsoever he remembered”.
1 Peter is written “By Silvanus, a faithful brother” (1 Pet 5:12). Our people data treats Silvanus as Paul’s companion Silas.

scripture.text: Jesus tells Peter that when he is old “another shall gird thee, and carry thee whither thou wouldest not”. John adds: “This spake he, signifying by what death he should glorify God” (John 21:18–19).

The writer of 2 Peter, who names himself “Simon Peter” (2 Pet 1:1), says “shortly I must put off this my tabernacle, even as our Lord Jesus Christ hath shewed me” (2 Pet 1:14). Who wrote 2 Peter is discussed on the Letters pages.
Acts last names him at the council in Jerusalem (Acts 15:7) and never says how, where or when he died.

items.q: When did Peter come to Rome, and how long was he there?
items.full: When did Peter come to Rome, and how long was he there?

views.label: He and Paul founded the Roman church together
views.holders: Dionysius of Corinth (about 170); Irenaeus (about 180)

argument.text: Irenaeus speaks of the church “founded and organized at Rome by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul”, who then “committed into the hands of Linus the office of the episcopate”. Neither writer says how long Peter stayed.

views.label: He came to Rome at the end of his life
views.holders: Origen (first half of the 3rd century), as reported by Eusebius

argument.text: After preaching in Asia Minor, Peter “at last, having come to Rome, he was crucified”.

views.label: He came under Claudius and led the church for twenty-five years
views.holders: Eusebius (about 325) for the arrival under Claudius; Jerome (392) for the twenty-five years

argument.text: Eusebius has Peter led to Rome “during the reign of Claudius”; Jerome dates it to “the second year of Claudius” and counts twenty-five years to Nero’s fourteenth year.

items.q: Was the man Paul opposed at Antioch the apostle Peter?
items.full: Was the man Paul opposed at Antioch the apostle Peter?

views.label: Yes, the apostle Peter
views.holders: Tertullian (about 200); the KJV text

argument.text: The KJV reads “Peter” in Galatians 2:11 and 2:14. Tertullian writes that “Peter was rebuked because, after he had lived with the Gentiles, he proceeded to separate himself from their company”.

views.label: No, another Cephas, one of the Seventy
views.holders: Clement of Alexandria (about 200), Hypotyposes book 5, as reported by Eusebius

argument.text: Clement “says that Cephas was one of the seventy disciples, a man who bore the same name as the apostle Peter”. Tischendorf’s Greek text in the site library reads “Cephas” in Galatians 2:11 and 2:14, where the KJV reads “Peter”.

items.q: Simon, Cephas, Peter: why three names?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: Jesus told Simon, “thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone” (John 1:42), and in Matthew, “thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church” (Matt 16:18). Paul uses both names for the same man in two neighbouring verses (Gal 2:8–9).

items.q: Jona, Jonas or John: who was his father?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: The KJV gives his father’s name as Jona or Jonas. Tischendorf’s Greek text in the site library reads ‘son of John’ at John 21:15, and our people data files the father under the name John.

items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: The “Simeon” of Acts 15:14 is taken to be Peter because James is replying to Peter’s speech just before (Acts 15:7–11). Our people data files the verse under Peter.

items.from: How the story ends: Scripture beside tradition, never blended

items.q: What do the early writers say about Mark, Peter and the Gospel?
items.full: What do the early writers say about Mark, Peter and the Gospel? (In date order; they do not agree on the details.)

views.label: Mark wrote down what Peter taught, “though not indeed in order”
views.holders: “The presbyter”, as quoted by Papias (early 2nd century), in Eusebius 3.39.15

argument.text: Mark “wrote down accurately, though not indeed in order, whatsoever he remembered of the things said or done by Christ.” “For he neither heard the Lord nor followed him, but afterward … he followed Peter”.

views.label: After Peter's and Paul's death
views.holders: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1 (about 180)

argument.text: “After their departure Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, also transmitted to us in writing those things which Peter had preached.”

views.label: At Rome in Peter's lifetime; Peter “neither directly forbade nor encouraged it”
views.holders: Clement of Alexandria, Hypotyposes (about 200), in Eusebius 6.14.6-7

argument.text: Hearers of Peter's preaching at Rome asked Mark, “who had followed him for a long time and remembered his sayings”, to write them out.

views.label: In Peter's lifetime, and with Peter's approval
views.holders: Origen (about 245 or later), in Eusebius 6.25.5; Eusebius himself (2.15, about 325); Jerome (392)

argument.text: Origen: Mark “composed it according to the instructions of Peter”. Eusebius says Peter “was pleased” and gave the work “the sanction of his authority”, citing Clement; McGiffert notes that this “contradicts the account of Clement”.

items.q: Did the apostle Peter write 2 Peter?
items.full: Did the apostle Peter write 2 Peter?
items.from: Asked on the James, Peter & Jude page

views.label: Doubted from early times
views.holders: Origen; Eusebius; Jerome

argument.text: Origen spoke of one acknowledged letter of Peter and perhaps a second, which was doubtful. Eusebius said the second letter was not received as canonical, though many found it useful and read it with the other Scriptures. Jerome reported that many thought it was not Peter's because its style differs from the first, and elsewhere explained the difference by Peter's using two different interpreters.

views.label: Written by the apostle Peter
views.holders: Zahn (by Peter's own hand, before 1 Peter); Bigg (genuine, the style differing because Peter used different helpers); Easton (1897); the ISBE, citing Salmon, Warfield and Zahn

argument.text: The writer's own claims — the coming death the Lord had shown him, the voice on the holy mount, "this second epistle" — together with words shared with 1 Peter and the early Hebrew form of the name, "Symeon".

views.label: Peter's teaching, set down by a disciple at his command
views.holders: John Calvin (1551)

argument.text: Calvin did not recognise Peter's own language in it, but found nothing unworthy of Peter, and thought one of his disciples wrote it at his direction.

views.label: A later writer using Peter's name
views.holders: Chase (about AD 150), as reported by the ISBE; J. B. Mayor (1907)

argument.text: Weak early attestation, a style unlike 1 Peter, and dependence on Jude; Mayor also thought the phrase "the holy mount" pointed to a later stage of tradition. Even so, Hort — as Mayor recalls — said that if asked he would judge the balance of argument against the letter, and the moment he had done so would begin to think he might be wrong.

items.from: Asked on the James, Peter & Jude page

views.label: Rome, called Babylon as a figure
views.holders: Papias and Clement of Alexandria, as reported by Eusebius; Bigg, who says the view was universal until the Reformation and still the most common; Mayor; Grotius, Whitby, Lardner and others named in the note by Calvin's editor

argument.text: Revelation calls Rome "Babylon"; a strong tradition places Peter in Rome; and Mark and Silvanus are not known to have gone east.

views.label: Babylon on the Euphrates
views.holders: Calvin; Erasmus; Beza, John Lightfoot, Adam Clarke and others named by Calvin's editor; Easton (1897); the ISBE

argument.text: Peter writes plainly, and a figurative place-name in a greeting would be odd; many Jews lived there. Calvin's editor noted that dating a letter by a figurative name has no other example in Scripture.

views.label: Babylon in Egypt, a Roman fortress at what is now Old Cairo
views.holders: Bishop Pearson, Mill and Le Clerc, as reported by Bigg and Calvin's editor

argument.text: A real place of that name existed. Against it, Bigg notes that in the first century it was only a large military post.

views.label: Jerusalem (or Joppa)
views.holders: Harnack ("possibly Rome, but more probably Jerusalem"); others mentioned by Bigg

argument.text: A figurative name for the city that rejected Christ.

items.q: When Peter wrote "by Silvanus", was Silvanus the carrier or the secretary?
items.full: When Peter wrote "by Silvanus", was Silvanus the carrier or the secretary?
items.from: Asked on the James, Peter & Jude page

views.label: The bearer of the letter
views.holders: The ISBE; Hort, who traces Silvanus's journey through the five regions

argument.text: The phrase most naturally names the man who carried the letter to its readers.

views.label: A secretary who shaped the Greek
views.holders: Bigg; Zahn, as Bigg reports

argument.text: If Peter used a helper to draft one letter, he likely did so as a rule — which would explain why 1 and 2 Peter read so differently.

items.q: Jude and 2 Peter share a run of the same material. Which came first?
items.full: Jude and 2 Peter share a run of the same material. Which came first?
items.from: Asked on the James, Peter & Jude page

views.label: Jude came first, and 2 Peter used it
views.holders: J. B. Mayor (1907), who lists Neander, Credner, Ewald, Hilgenfeld, Holtzmann, Harnack, Bernhard Weiss, Abbott, Farrar, Salmon and Chase; Bigg adds Reuss, Jülicher and von Soden. The ISBE allows that perhaps a majority favour it

argument.text: 2 Peter's unexplained remark about angels who bring no railing accusation reads like a riddle whose answer is Michael in Jude 9; "darkness reserved" suits Jude's wandering stars better than 2 Peter's wells; and 2 Peter drops Jude's material from Enoch. Mayor doubted that anyone would gather scattered phrases from 2 Peter to build Jude's tight cluster of images.

views.label: 2 Peter came first, and Jude used it
views.holders: Luther; Lumby, Mansel, Plummer, Spitta and Zahn (as listed by Bigg); Bigg himself; the ISBE, following Zahn. Döllinger held it and later gave it up

argument.text: 2 Peter speaks of false teachers still to come, Jude of men already present; Jude's "before of old ordained" and his call to remember the apostles' words may point back to 2 Peter; and the greater figure, Peter, is less likely to be the borrower.

views.label: A middle position
views.holders: Kühl, as reported by Bigg

argument.text: 2 Peter 2:1–3:2 is an insertion, taken from Jude, into an earlier letter that Jude had himself used. Bigg called this kind of solution a last resort.

views.label: Both drew on a common source
views.holders: Raised as a possibility and set aside by the ISBE

argument.text: The shared material would come from a third writing now lost; the ISBE notes that nothing from antiquity hints at one.

items.q: When were these four letters written?
items.full: When were these four letters written?
items.from: Asked on the James, Peter & Jude page

views.label: James: the 40s AD, before the Jerusalem council
views.holders: Mayor; Schaff; Plumptre, Alford, Zahn, Dods and others listed by the ISBE

argument.text: No Gentile question and no circumcision debate; no mention of the fall of Jerusalem.

views.label: James: about 60–62, late in James's life
views.holders: Easton; Wiesinger, Farrar and others listed by the ISBE

argument.text: Settled congregations, and the Lord's coming has been delayed long enough to call for patience.

views.label: James: after his death, AD 70–150
views.holders: Baur, Harnack, Jülicher, Bacon and others listed by the ISBE

argument.text: Good Greek, little explicit Christian doctrine, and a supposed reaction to Paul.

views.label: 1 Peter: AD 58–64, before Nero's persecution
views.holders: Bigg

argument.text: Hostility from neighbours, but no persecution by the state yet.

views.label: 1 Peter: about AD 64, under Nero
views.holders: The ISBE

argument.text: Everything in the letter is read as pointing to Nero's time.

views.label: 1 Peter: AD 83–93, not by Peter
views.holders: Harnack, as reported by Bigg

argument.text: Paul's influence and the lack of personal detail.

views.label: 2 Peter: about AD 60–63
views.holders: Zahn, as reported by Bigg

argument.text: Written by Peter himself, before 1 Peter.

views.label: 2 Peter: shortly before Peter's death, mid-60s
views.holders: Easton; the ISBE; Calvin

argument.text: The writer says his death is near.

views.label: 2 Peter: about AD 150, or later
views.holders: Chase, as reported by the ISBE; Mayor, who weighed several second-century dates

argument.text: Weak early attestation and dependence on Jude.

views.label: Jude: about 65 to 80
views.holders: Bigg (not much after 65); Easton (66 or 70); Zahn (70–75); Mayor and Lumby (about 80); Chase (not later than 80); Salmon (before 81)

argument.text: Zahn read verse 5 as a sign that Jerusalem had already fallen.

views.label: Jude: AD 100–180
views.holders: Jülicher, as reported by Bigg; Pfleiderer argued for the mid-second century, which Bigg rejected

argument.text: The intruders are taken to be second-century teachers.

items.q: Scripture never says that Peter went to Rome, or how, where or when he died.
Acts does not say where “another place” was when Peter left Jerusalem after his escape (Acts 12:17).
Paul’s greetings to the church at Rome (Romans 16:3–16) do not name Peter.
Scripture does not name Peter’s wife and does not mention children.
Scripture does not give Peter’s age at any point.

notSaid: Scripture never says that Peter went to Rome, or how, where or when he died.

Scripture does not give Peter’s age at any point.
